name: Ubiquinone (topical coenzyme Q10)
lead: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble, quinone compound found in cell membranes and involved in mitochondrial electron transport, and it also acts as an antioxidant. [13] It is included in some anti-aging creams, and the literature describes cosmetically applied CoQ10 as having been reported to reduce photoaging and wrinkle depth, while noting that its bioavailability through skin is poor. [2]

Formulation research has therefore focused on delivery systems such as liposomes. [2] Most controlled human trials of topical CoQ10 identified in the sources reviewed are in oral or eye conditions rather than facial aging. [8][10]
infobox: Isolated 1957 from beef heart mitochondria; structure reported 1958 [13]

paras: CoQ10 has a benzoquinone head and a ten-unit isoprenoid tail, is orange-yellow, and exists in oxidized, semiquinone and reduced (ubiquinol) states. [13] A compound first isolated in 1950 from horse intestinal lining was later identified as the same family, and in 1966 a study reported that the reduced form acts as an antioxidant in cells. [13]
A 2010 paper described preparing a liposomal CoQ10 formulation for topical application, stating that bioavailability of topical CoQ10 is poor and that practical formulations are desirable. [2]
Oral CoQ10 is generally well tolerated according to Wikipedia, with occasional gastrointestinal upset, rashes and headache. [13] Topical-specific safety data are not described in these sources.

No trials of topical CoQ10 for facial wrinkles or aging were found in the sources reviewed. Human trials of topical CoQ10 exist in other settings: a randomized trial compared it with a topical corticosteroid in symptomatic oral lichen planus, and a triple-blinded pilot trial examined it for early wound healing after gum recession surgery. [8][10] A small study reported eye drops combining CoQ10 and vitamin E in retinopathy of prematurity. [9]
Animal research includes diabetic mouse wound healing with low-level light and topical CoQ10, and rodent eye studies of neuroprotection. [4][1][3]

card.summary: The mitochondrial antioxidant in many anti-aging creams; skin penetration is a recognized hurdle and direct wrinkle trials are scarce.
card.note: Topical trials found are in oral or eye conditions, not facial aging.

quick.overview:
Coenzyme Q10 is a compound the body makes in mitochondria, and it is added to anti-aging creams for antioxidant effects. One formulation paper says cosmetic CoQ10 has been reported to reduce photoaging, but that skin bioavailability is poor.

Human trials of topical CoQ10 identified here concern oral and eye conditions rather than wrinkles.
quick.mechanism: It carries electrons in the mitochondrial chain and its reduced form acts as an antioxidant. Delivery systems such as liposomes have been studied to improve skin uptake.
quick.risks: Oral CoQ10 is described as generally well tolerated. Topical-specific safety data were not found, and it is sold as a cosmetic or supplement rather than an approved anti-aging drug.
